articles.title: ‘Seismic shift’: World reacts to US midterm election results - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: ‘Seismic shift’: World reacts to US midterm election results  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
Democrats in the United States have scored a major victory in midterm elections, taking control of both chambers of Congress in a stinging rebuke of President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.
The results are being carefully watched outside the US, as foreign leaders consider how the new political reality in Washington could affect US foreign policy – from the conflict with Iran to the Russia-Ukraine war and trade relations.
Trump himself has acknowledged the US-Israel war on Iran likely impacted his party’s poor performance in the elections, saying voters were probably not ready “for the short-term consequence of the price of gasoline”.
Here are the latest reactions from world leaders, as the scale of the Democratic victory continues to emerge:
European Union
European Parliament Vice President Christel Schaldemose said the US results left her “cautiously optimistic on Europe’s behalf”.
“Not because everything now changes for the better, but because it could benefit the support for Ukraine, the green transition, and relations with the rest of the world,” said Schaldemose in a post on X.
“But the EU must continue the course of standing stronger and standing on its own two feet. That’s not up for debate,” she added.
Iran
Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who is also the chief negotiator in talks with the US, said voters had rejected conflict.
“Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” wrote Ghalibaf in a post on X.
“If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” he added.
Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile, said partisan shifts in Washington would not alter the US’s “hostility” towards Tehran.
“If there are still those who harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system could change through party or factional shifts, or who believe that making concessions to the US could persuade it to abandon its hostility towards the Iranian people, they are gravely mistaken,” said Khamenei in a statement shared by Iranian state media.
Israel
There was no immediate reaction from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, a Trump ally whose coalition lost its own majority in Israel’s parliament in elections last week.
However, opposition figure Yair Golan, whose party is in a coalition seeking to replace Netanyahu, said the US vote reveals “just how toxic Netanyahu has become” among US Democrats and Republicans alike.
He warned that if Netanyahu and his far-right government remain in power, Israel would be on “a path toward international sanctions, global isolation, and a confrontation with the United States – our most important friend and ally.”
Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid, also part of the anti-Netanyahu coalition, said the US vote effectively ruled out “any possibility of a unity government led by Netanyahu”.
Germany
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz suggested that, having lost control of Congress, Trump is likely to bypass it by using executive orders.
“Trump has, for the past two years, largely governed without consulting Congress,” Merz remarked. “Why should things be any different now?”
Berlin’s Defence Minister Boris Pistorius congratulated the Democratic Party on a “historic victory”, but reiterated that Europe must continue to raise its game regarding looking after its own security.
United Kingdom
Health Minister James Frith stressed that the UK would maintain steady, strong ties with Washington despite an apparent “seismic shift in domestic politics for the Americans”.
“The change of emphasis of power in the States is frequent,” Frith told British media. “But the mainstay of the relationship with the UK Government, as its closest ally, is unwavering and unchanging.”
“So I don’t expect it to change the nature of the relationship at all; it remains very strong,” he added.
France
Finance Minister Roland Lescure said France would wait to see whether Trump, who remains in control of US foreign policy, adjusts his approach.
“Either he decides to rise above the fray – acknowledging that changes are necessary, particularly regarding gasoline prices, which directly affect people – and, I might add, he tones down his international involvement, or he does not,” Lescure told French TV. “Frankly, this is something we will need to keep an eye on in the coming days.”
Spain
Left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the US Democrats’ landslide victory was emblematic of the “unravelling” of the global far right.
“It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will soon happen in Spain,” said Sanchez, whose own premiership is at stake in snap elections he called for November 29.
Sanchez said US voters had rejected policies that “only impoverish”, as well as hate, sexism, climate change denialism and “the privileges of the elites”.
Greece
Government spokesman Pavlos Marinakis said US-Greek relations would not be affected by the election results.
“Greek-American relations will remain strong,” he told local media. “The United States is our strategic ally, and this will continue for major projects and all major agreements. Nothing will be affected by this outcome. It is obvious that we respect every outcome. The conclusions are clear.”
Russia
Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov stressed the need to wait for the final results of US elections to come into focus, but noted that leaders in the US Democratic Party had a “sharply negative” approach to relations with Moscow.
Russia’s position on Ukraine and broader foreign policy “is not based on short-term considerations and, naturally, does not depend on the fluctuations of the political barometer in other countries,” Ryabkov was quoted by Russian state media as saying.
“We will continue our work in accordance with the directives of the President of the Russian Federation,” he added.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow hoped the US midterm results would not impact Trump’s “peacemaking efforts”.
China
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Beijing would continue its “constructive strategic relationship” with the US, stressing that US elections are a “domestic affair”.
“China is willing to work with the US to safeguard and implement the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, strengthen communication, properly manage differences and expand cooperation, build a constructive strategic relationship based on respect and equality,” Mao told reporters in Beijing.
Japan
Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said whatever the outcome of the US vote, “the Japan-US alliance is the cornerstone of Japan’s foreign and security policy”.
“As the international situation becomes turbulent and increasingly uncertain, a strong Japan-US alliance is essential for maximising Japan’s national interests and for peace and stability in the international community,” Kihara said at a press briefing.
South Africa
President Cyril Ramaphosa, who has clashed with Trump over the US president’s promotion of debunked claims of a white genocide in South Africa, said the election marks “a new era in world relations”.
“We have seen that the Democrats have taken control of the Senate and of the House, and the people of America have spoken,” Ramaphosa told reporters.

articles.title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports - BBC
articles.summary: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports  BBC
articles.full_text:
The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month.
The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday.
Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders.
The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market.
As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.
Speaking during the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, the prime minister said a UK-EU deal could add up to 0.4% extra on GDP.
The deal could have the following impact:
- Exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes would be able to resume
- It should remove the need for £200 Export Health Certificates, which confirm the product meets the health requirements of the country it is heading to
- It should also end the need for £25 Phytosanitary certificates, which show that plants or plant products are free from pests and diseases
- Inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU could be removed
- It will bring back passports for British pets being taken into the EU
In return, the UK is expected to commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards - a process called "dynamic alignment".
Each of the elements on the table was up for discussion under Sir Keir Starmer, and the summit would have taken place by now had Labour not replaced its leader in July.
Under Andy Burnham, Britain's approach to post-Brexit relations with the EU have shifted significantly. Sir Keir said the UK would not rejoin the bloc in his lifetime, while Burnham has said he would like to see Britain back in the EU in his.
At Chogm on Tuesday, Burnham said: "I think people in Britain would expect me to take that with both hands, given where we've been in recent times, and that's what I'm doing."
Pressed on whether it would be acceptable for the UK to have its rules on food trade made by the EU, he said: "We're not in the EU, therefore we do have to work with them in a different way.
"But if that can get growth, if that can help our farmers, if that can remove red tape from British businesses, I think most people would expect me to go to that summit and negotiate the best deal that I can.
"And that's what I've been doing in recent weeks, leaning in, being positive, having a really constructive relationship with our European partners and hopefully we can land a good deal for Britain in terms of growth but also I hope more collaboration on controlling immigration."
Jon Walsh, the chief executive and co-founder of Bio&Me, which makes granolas, mueslis and yoghurts, told BBC 5 Live the draft deal sounded like "really good news".
"We're just a small company but when we were trying to export our yoghurts before, every time we'd send a pallet we had to pay a vet to inspect it and that was £140, and that meant that you'd lose money... so we had to stop."
The company also had problems exporting granola and overnight oats, with some shipments being returned.
"It was so frustrating because it was the same person filling out the same form and yet half would make it through and half wouldn't," Walsh said.
"You just kind of give up because you're losing money."
In an interview with ITV, Burnham said "public opinion has changed nationally" since the 2016 Brexit vote, but added he would "not run ahead of public opinion" on the issue.
"The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit," he added.
Burnham also said he had not proposed the return of freedom of movement between the UK and EU.
Asked by the BBC about the UK's relationship with the EU, Tory Leader Kemi Badenoch said that while we should "work closely", "dynamic alignment" with the EU would be a red line and "actually take us backwards".
Liberal Democrat Europe spokesperson Al Pinkerton said the draft deal was a "patch, not a fix".
"The real solution is to rejoin the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU," he added.
Reform UK's business spokesman Richard Tice said: "One of the key benefits of Brexit was that Britain no longer had to adhere to ridiculous EU rules.
"Returning to any form of alignment with Europe would crush Britain's competitiveness and force us to surrender sovereignty over trade policy, putting trade deals worth hundreds of billions of pounds at risk."
While UK rules remain mostly aligned with EU ones, there are some areas where England has diverged from the EU rule book, for example on "precision breeding" of plants, previously known as gene editing. In recent weeks, agreement has been struck on transition arrangements while the EU's new regulations come in to force.
The government has already announced a European Partnerships Bill which will provide a legal mechanism for the application of new EU rules and regulations. This will also allow for the necessary alignments for the linking of the UK emissions trading scheme with the EU's, and save the need for UK exporters to pay the EU's new carbon border tax.
The draft agreements will be discussed at a meeting of EU ambassadors called Coreper on Wednesday, with some key details on the planned numbers in a Youth Experience Scheme to be finalised at a political level in the coming days. A discount on full foreign student fees for EU students is likely to be pushed to next year alongside a plan to reconnect electricity markets.
The BBC understands the draft agreements will also include some references to UK involvement in defence co-operation schemes, access to law enforcement databases and some reassurances over the EU's "Made in Europe" plans.
A food deal will have particular significance for Northern Ireland, radically reducing the impact of the post-Brexit Irish Sea border.
Northern Ireland's Brexit deal kept it inside the EU's single market for goods. That means food products from elsewhere in the UK require paperwork and some physical checks when arriving at NI's ports. A deal will ultimately end those requirements.
While the food trade plans have been backed by supermarkets and farmers representatives, some pro-Brexit campaigners have criticised the reapplication of EU rules. The post-Brexit trade deal signed by Boris Johnson's government prioritised regulatory freedoms for the UK over avoiding new regulatory red tape, checks and delays.
But William Bain, the British Chamber of Commerce's (BCC) head of trade policy, told the BBC's Today programme that business overall thought it was a "price is worth paying" to follow common rules, as companies would benefit from "lower costs, reduced delays [and] increased market access".
At the moment, he said, the requirement for Export Health Certificates can add thousands of pounds of costs to each truck carrying goods, in addition "to the delays that people find at the ports or at the borders".
"So we get lower exports because of the delays and the massive increases in costs that have come into the supply chain."
The BCC has released a new analysis of its members' views suggesting options for a closer relationship.
The business lobby group says the current trade relationship is "failing to deliver", leaving firms "struggling with a thicket of Brexit red tape" nearly six years after the UK's exit from the bloc.

articles.title: Meet the EU's New Ambassador to Mexico — and the Trade Deal Defining Her Mission - Latin Times
articles.summary: Meet the EU's New Ambassador to Mexico — and the Trade Deal Defining Her Mission  Latin Times
articles.full_text:
A newly designated EU envoy formally launched her diplomatic mission in Mexico City on Monday, stepping into a bilateral relationship that has undergone its deepest transformation in more than two decades — and inheriting a ratification race that will define her entire tenure.
Belén Martínez Carbonell, who served as Secretary-General of the European External Action Service since February 2025, presented copies of her letters of credence to Jonathan Chait, head of Protocol at Mexico's Secretariat of Foreign Affairs, on November 3. The step formally activated her authority as the bloc's top representative in the country.
A Seasoned Diplomat Steps Down From Brussels — and Up to Mexico City
Martínez Carbonell brings more than three decades of EU institutional experience to the posting. The Spanish diplomat, born in Ourense in 1969, built her career across both the European Commission and the EEAS, rising to serve as the number two to High Representative Kaja Kallas and coordinating the EU's entire internal foreign policy apparatus before transitioning to her new assignment.
She replaces Francisco André, the Portuguese diplomat who served as EU representative in Mexico from September 2024 and who took office as EU Ambassador to Brazil on September 3, 2026. André departed with an unusually personal farewell, describing his travels from Tijuana to Cancún as formative experiences and declaring the EU-Mexico relationship "stronger than ever." The groundwork he laid hands Martínez Carbonell a foundation built on momentum — but the structural work of full treaty implementation remains ahead.
She set an optimistic tone from the start, writing on X after presenting her credentials: "¡Qué alegría estar en México! Con mucha ilusión, comienzo mi misión como Embajadora de la UE en México, con el compromiso de seguir fortaleciendo los lazos entre la UE y México."
The Trade Overhaul at the Center of Her Mandate
The Modernized Global Agreement is the defining commercial event of the current EU-Mexico relationship. Signed on May 22, 2026, at the two sides' first bilateral summit in eleven years — held at Mexico City's National Palace — the MGA replaces a framework that has governed ties since 2000 and that has already driven bilateral goods trade to approximately $88.2 billion in 2025, up from a fraction of that figure when the original accord entered into force.
The scale of the update is significant. The agreement eliminates tariffs on 99% of products, opens up agricultural trade in both directions, and extends protection to 568 EU geographical indications — traditional European food and drink products, from Prosciutto di Parma to Manchego cheese, that will now be legally shielded from counterfeiting and imitation in Mexican markets. The EU is Mexico's second-largest investor, with foreign direct investment reaching approximately $9.9 billion in 2025.
Parliament Said Yes — Now Comes the Hard Part
The European Parliament cleared the agreement on July 8, 2026, approving it by 479 votes to 119, with 65 abstentions — clearing one of the highest institutional hurdles in the process. The EU Council subsequently adopted the decision to formally conclude the faster-tracked Interim Trade Agreement on July 14. But full implementation of the broader Modernized Global Agreement still requires ratification by all 27 EU national parliaments and Mexico's Senate.
Mexico's Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard argued after the European Parliament vote that the agreement could enter into force within the same year once the Mexican Senate completes its own ratification process. On the diplomatic side, Esteban Moctezuma Barragán — the former Mexican ambassador to the United States — was confirmed as Mexico's new ambassador to the EU, Belgium, and Luxembourg in July 2026, and has been coordinating Mexico's ratification strategy across European capitals ever since.
Alignment on Both Sides — the Question Is Speed
That coordinated push gives Martínez Carbonell a counterpart equally focused on turning a signed text into an operating commercial reality. With a confirmed Mexican envoy in Brussels and a veteran EU diplomat in Mexico City, the institutional architecture is in place. The question her tenure will answer is whether that alignment can compress a ratification timeline that has historically stretched across years — and in some cases, across a decade.
